methodSummary: Contract Gross = Rate × Hours × Weeks. Unpaid vacation, holidays and bench time are modeled only here, via Weeks/Year.
True Equivalent = Contract Gross × (1 - Overhead %) - fixed annual costs (advanced mode). Overhead covers only costs not already captured by fewer billable weeks.
Break-even Hourly Rate = the minimum rate at which the True Equivalent matches the Employee Salary.
assumptions: The overhead percentage covers additional contractor costs excluding unpaid vacation, holidays, and non-billable weeks (those are captured by 'Weeks/Year'): the employer share of payroll taxes, health insurance, missed retirement matching, and business expenses.
Calculates comparative gross equivalence. Exact net tax outcomes may slightly differ.
insights: The most common mistake contractors make is setting their overhead percent to 0. A documented baseline is 20-30% for the costs not already covered by fewer billable weeks: employer-share payroll taxes, health insurance, retirement match, and business expenses.
If the 'Difference %' is less than +15%, the stability of the employee role might make it more valuable than the contract.

faqs.q: What should I enter for Self-Employment Overhead?
faqs.a: Usually 20-30%. Enter only costs not already covered by your reduced Weeks/Year: the employer half of US payroll taxes (7.65% is a documented default for the extra burden versus an employee; the exact figure varies with income thresholds and deductions), health insurance premiums, skipped retirement matching, and business costs such as software, insurance, and accounting. Do not include vacation, holidays, or other unpaid weeks here - those belong in 'Weeks/Year'.

faqs.q: Why is 'Contractor True Equivalent' lower than 'Gross Revenue'?
faqs.a: Because Gross Revenue is business cash flow, not your salary. The True Equivalent backs out the business costs your employer normally pays.

faqs.q: Do I need to account for software or hardware expenses?
faqs.a: Yes. If you must buy your own laptop and software licenses as a contractor, mentally raise the overhead percentage to compensate.

faqs.q: Why is standard salaried PTO omitted from the employee side?
faqs.a: Because the employee receives the full salary regardless of taking the 4 weeks PTO. The contractor loses billable hours when taking PTO, which is handled via 'Weeks/Year'.

faqs.q: If the difference is negative, should I avoid contracting?
faqs.a: Mathematically yes. A negative difference means you are taking on all the business risk of contracting while effectively taking a pay cut.

faqs.q: Does this tool work for international remote jobs?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as you factor the local self-employment compliance costs into the overhead percentage precisely.

faqs.q: How much more should a contractor make than an employee?
faqs.a: At minimum about 30% more per hour just to break even on the employer share of payroll taxes and lost benefits. Realistically 50-100% more once you price in health insurance, retirement, and the weeks you cannot bill. The Break-even Hourly Rate output shows the exact floor for your own numbers.

faqs.q: Is contractor pay higher than employee pay?
faqs.a: The headline rate usually is; the take-home often is not. A contractor's gross hourly rate typically runs 30-100% above the equivalent salaried rate, but after self-employment costs and unbilled weeks the net advantage can disappear. Compare the 'Contractor True Equivalent' output - not gross revenue - against the salary.

faqs.q: What is the difference between contract and direct hire salary?
faqs.a: Direct hire means a permanent W-2 salary with benefits, employer-paid payroll taxes, and paid time off. A contract role pays a higher headline rate, but you carry those costs yourself. A $100,000 direct-hire salary works out to roughly $48/hour over 2,080 hours; a comparable contract rate for the same work is typically $65-75/hour or more.

faqs.q: How do I compare a salary to a contractor rate?
faqs.a: Convert the salary to an effective hourly value (salary divided by 2,080 hours), then convert the contract rate to a true equivalent: rate times billable hours and weeks, minus the costs an employer would otherwise carry. This calculator does that conversion and reports the difference in dollars and percent.

richContent:
How much does a contractor make?

Independent contractors generally earn a higher gross hourly rate than salaried employees, but their net take-home pay is often lower than it appears. To match the lifestyle of a $100k employee, a contractor typically needs to gross $130k to $150k annually. A $50/hour W-2 salary requires a $65 to $75/hour 1099 contract rate just to break even.

Employee Salary vs Contractor Hourly Rate

You cannot directly compare an employee salary to a contractor hourly rate. An employee is paid for 52 weeks regardless of holidays, sick days, or slow periods. A contractor is paid strictly for billable hours worked. Therefore, 2,000 standard working hours rarely equal 2,000 billable contract hours. You must discount your expected hours to account for admin work and unpaid time off.

Taxes and Benefits Differences

Factor Employee (W-2) Contractor (1099)
Taxes (US) Employer pays half FICA You pay the full 15.3% (the extra burden vs an employee is the 7.65% employer half)
PTO & Sick Leave Paid Unpaid (lost revenue)
Insurance & Perks Subsidized by employer 100% out-of-pocket

What Overhead to Assume

When using this calculator, a documented default for Self-Employment Overhead is 20% to 30%: the employer half of payroll taxes (7.65% in the US - a default, not a universal figure, since thresholds and deductions shift the exact burden), the cost of acquiring your own health insurance (often 5-10% of gross), and missing 401(k) matches (3-5%). If you also purchase your own software licenses, equipment, and liability insurance, push the assumption toward 30%. Do not include unpaid vacation or holidays in overhead - reduce 'Weeks/Year' instead, otherwise the same cost is counted twice.

Break-Even Formula

Contractor True Equivalent = (Hourly Rate × Billable Hours/Week × Working Weeks/Year) × (1 - Overhead %)

The calculator reports this directly as the Break-even Hourly Rate: the minimum rate at which your True Equivalent matches the Employee Base Salary. If your target client won't approve that rate, you are effectively taking a pay cut to become a contractor. Use the advanced mode to itemize taxes, insurance, retirement, and business costs instead of a single percentage.
